name: Grapefruit and grapefruit juice
short: Raises levels of some medicines. Case reports: torsade on amiodarone, opioid toxicity on methadone, rhabdomyolysis on atorvastatin. Trial: juice alone lengthened QT. Linked to kidney stones.
text: Medicine interactions (case reports): a woman given amiodarone for atrial fibrillation developed marked QT prolongation and ventricular arrhythmias, including torsade de pointes that needed immediate electrical cardioversion; she had been drinking large amounts of grapefruit juice regularly, and the authors attribute the effect to grapefruit juice blocking the breakdown of amiodarone. A 51-year-old man taking daily methadone was found unresponsive, with low oxygen, slowed breathing and pinpoint pupils, and needed repeated naloxone; he had drunk about 500 mL of grapefruit juice a day for 3 days, and the authors call this the first reported case in which the interaction caused an opioid toxidrome (opioid poisoning). A 2008 report of four cases of rhabdomyolysis (muscle breakdown) with unusual causes lists an interaction between grapefruit juice and atorvastatin among them. In kidney transplant recipients, one report describes an approximately 2-fold rise in tacrolimus levels, with no change in dose, attributed to eating grapefruit in hospital; another describes a sixfold rise to 30 µg/L the morning after about a litre of blood orange juice followed by a supervised 250 mL dose of grapefruit juice that was given deliberately to raise his low tacrolimus levels, with kidney biopsy findings consistent with a drug-related inflammatory reaction; tacrolimus was stopped for a time, and the authors say causality is unconfirmed. A 2006 review lists statins (HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors), calcium antagonists and immunosuppressants among the drug classes known to interact with grapefruit. Heart rhythm (the juice itself): in an open-label randomised crossover study with blinded outcome evaluation, 2 L of grapefruit juice taken in divided doses by 30 healthy volunteers prolonged their rate-corrected QT interval about as much as moxifloxacin, the medicine the study used for comparison, and the study reports a net prolongation from grapefruit of 14.0 ms (the abstract does not say whether this figure covers the healthy volunteers only); the effect was greater in female participants and reached a net 21.8 ms in 10 patients with congenital long QT syndrome, who were tested with grapefruit juice only. Blood pressure medicine (single case): in a 50-year-old man with high blood pressure, 500 mL of grapefruit juice taken with nifedipine rapidly raised its blood level and lowered blood pressure for a short time, while it had no effect on the blood level of amlodipine (the abstract gives no blood pressure result for amlodipine), and eating one grapefruit before the medicine had no effect on either drug. Studies in healthy volunteers: double-strength grapefruit juice taken three times a day raised lovastatin peak levels about 12-fold and total exposure 15-fold (10 volunteers), simvastatin about 9-fold and 16-fold (10 volunteers), and atorvastatin acid exposure 2.5-fold (12 volunteers), but had no effect on pravastatin (11 volunteers); a meta-analysis of 7 randomised trials of citrus juices in healthy volunteers found that grapefruit juice raised exposure to the immunosuppressant cyclosporine by about 53% (the abstract does not say how many of the 7 trials tested grapefruit juice); it raised sildenafil exposure by 23% in 24 men while peak levels were essentially unchanged; and it had no clinically relevant effect on ambrisentan or bosentan in 28 volunteers. On the other side, in 130 patients on long-term atorvastatin who drank 300 mL of grapefruit juice a day for 90 days, atorvastatin levels rose by 19% to 26% in those who kept the same dose, with no adverse effects on liver tests or creatine phosphokinase (a muscle enzyme). Kidney stones (observational): in two large cohorts of people with no history of stones, each daily 240 mL serving of grapefruit juice was associated with a 44% higher risk of a first stone in 81,093 women and a 37% higher risk in 45,289 men; these are associations, not proof of cause, and in 10 healthy adults, 7 days of grapefruit juice raised urine oxalate and citrate but produced no net change in calculated stone-forming supersaturation.
